Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well" (Psalm 139:13-14). Here is why God knows you so exhaustively: he *made* you, and not at arm's length. He knit you together — stitch by careful stitch, in the hidden dark, before another human being on earth knew you existed. "Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them" (Psalm 139:16). The God who sees clean through you is the God who designed you, who watched you take shape when you were not yet shaped, who wrote out the days of your life before you had lived even one of them. This is the same word God spoke to Jeremiah before sending him out: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you" (Jeremiah 1:5). The exhaustive knowing of this psalm is not the cold gaze of a watcher. It is the tender, total knowledge of a Maker for the thing he made with his own hands and loves.

Here is where it lands on me, and I suspect on you. I spend a real amount of energy curating a version of myself for God to look at — the cleaned-up draft, the managed face I bring into prayer, the parts of me I have decided are presentable enough to bring into the light, while I keep the rest in the dark and hope he is looking elsewhere. And this psalm tells me the whole project is not just doomed but absurd. He has already read the unedited manuscript, cover to cover. He knew the very worst of me before I ever learned to hide it, and he knit me together anyway, and he writes my days anyway, and his hand holds me at the far edge of the sea anyway. We exhaust ourselves performing for a God who has already seen, in full, the thing behind the performance. The fear running through the first half of this psalm is the universal fear of being completely known. And the mercy running through the second half is that being completely known did not, in the end, make him turn away.

And that is exactly why the psalm ends not by running from the searching God but by handing him the lamp and asking for more of the search. "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!" (Psalm 139:23-24). The man who began the psalm overwhelmed and hemmed in by God's knowledge ends it inviting that knowledge all the way in, holding still for the examination, asking the One who sees everything to find what is wrong and lead him home. He can pray that — and so can we — because the One who knows absolutely everything about you is the One from whom nothing "in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39). And when your own heart rises up to condemn you, when you are sure that if God really saw you he could not love you, the gospel turns the terror of this psalm into its comfort: "we shall reassure our heart before him... for God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything" (1 John 3:19-20). He knows everything — and that, it turns out, is not the threat. That is the rescue.

You are fully known and held.

## Let Everything That Has Breath
*The Bible's prayerbook does not end with a request. It ends with five unbroken hallelujahs.*

**Text:** Psalms 146-150 · **Supporting:** Revelation 5:13 · Psalm 150:6 · Romans 11:36 · Revelation 7:9-10

A book that opened with one blessed man standing at a fork in the road closes with every breathing thing on earth lifting a single sound. The Psalter has prayed its way through everything a human life can hold — lament and confession, exile and terror, doubt that nearly slipped, the cry of dereliction from the bottom of the dark. It has held nothing back. And after all of it, the songbook of the people of God does not end with one more request, one more *how long*, one more plea for help. It ends with praise that will not stop, stacked five psalms deep.

**Five songs that begin and end the same way.**
Each of the last five psalms opens and closes with the same single word: *Hallelujah* — "Praise the LORD." Open Psalm 146, it is the first word; close it, it is the last. The same for 147, 148, 149, 150. That is not an accident of editing or a pious habit. It is the deliberate design of the whole collection. After all the honest *how longs* and *have mercies* and *why have you forsaken me*, the prayerbook of the people of God resolves into one held note, sustained across five psalms without a break, and the note is praise. "Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, O my soul! I will praise the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being" (Psalm 146:1-2). Notice that the man does not wait to feel like praising. He turns and addresses his own soul and *commands* it: praise the LORD, O my soul. Praise, in the Psalter, is not first a feeling that conveniently arrives. It is a thing the believer summons — deliberately, as a decision — while he still has breath in his body to summon it.

**The widening circle.**
And watch where the praise goes once it starts, because the movement across these five psalms is the whole point. It begins small and intimate — *praise the LORD, O my soul* — one man, one soul, addressing himself. And then it widens, psalm by psalm, until it has swallowed the entire created order. It pulls in the angels and the armies of heaven: "Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts!" (Psalm 148:2). It pulls in the sun and the moon and the stars: "Praise him, sun and moon, praise him, all you shining stars! Praise him, you highest heavens, and you waters above the heavens!" (Psalm 148:3-4). It pulls in the sea creatures and the wild weather and the mountains and the trees: "Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and mist, stormy wind fulfilling his word! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars!" (Psalm 148:7-9). And then it pulls in the whole human race, every rank and every age — "Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth! Young men and maidens together, old men and children! Let them praise the name of the LORD" (Psalm 148:11-13). The circle keeps opening, ring after ring — one soul, then the gathered congregation, then the nations, then the animals, then the weather, then the stars — until there is nothing left anywhere in creation that stands outside the song.

**The last line, and the only requirement.**
And then comes the final verse of the entire book of Psalms — the last word of a collection that has carried the full weight of every human sorrow and every human hope across one hundred and fifty songs: "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!" (Psalm 150:6). Read the entrance requirement carefully, because the whole gospel of the Psalter is hiding in it. Not *let everything that is happy praise the LORD.* Not *let everything that has had its prayers answered.* Not *let everything that has finally understood why,* or *let everything that has had a good year.* "Everything that has breath." The single, solitary qualification for praise is a pulse. If you are breathing, you are summoned. The book that began, back in Psalm 1, by dividing all of humanity into two ways and two destinies ends by gathering every last thing that breathes into one chorus.

Here is where I am exposed by this ending, and you are too. We treat praise as the thing we will get around to once the lament is finally resolved — once the prayer is answered, once the trouble lifts, once the diagnosis comes back clean, once we feel like it. We make our worship conditional on our circumstances. And the deliberate shape of the Psalter rebukes that order to its face. The book walks straight through every kind of darkness for a hundred and forty-nine psalms — it does not skip the valley, it does not pretend the forsakenness away — and then it ends, on purpose, on praise that depends on nothing whatsoever except breath. We withhold our worship until our situation has earned it from us. The last psalm says the breath in your lungs right now is reason enough, because the breath itself is a gift, on loan, from the very One being praised. To breathe and not praise is to take the gift and forget the Giver. Every exhale you spend on complaint and never on worship is borrowed air.

And the reason the Psalter can end this confident — this loud, this universal, this sure — is that the whole book has been pointing the entire way to One whose worship gathers a crowd no one could ever number. John, at the end of the Bible, saw the far edge of this widening circle, the place all five hallelujahs were always heading: "every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, 'To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!'" (Revelation 5:13). The five hallelujahs at the close of the Psalter are a rehearsal for that day. One day the single soul, the gathered congregation, the nations, the animals, the stars, and all creation will sing the note together, with one voice, before the throne and before the Lamb — "a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages" (Revelation 7:9-10) — because in the end "from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever" (Romans 11:36). The book that began with one blessed man ends with every breath, because that is where it was always going, and that is where you are going too, if you are breathing.

Every breath ends in praise.
